title: Dynasaurs: Efficient Universal Dynamic zkSNARKs from Sparse Linear Arguments
authors: Martí Batista, Álvaro Montes, Nikitas Paslis, and Carla Ràfols
abstract:
Dynamic zkSNARKs were recently introduced by Wang et al. [Eurocrypt, 2026]. This primitive extends standard zkSNARKs with an update algorithm that adapts a proof to a new statement in time sublinear in the circuit size, provided the witness changes in few positions. However, existing constructions either need a circuit-specific setup or, in the universal case, send over $130$ group elements and require over $180$ pairings.

As is the case for universal zkSNARKs, dynamic ones can be built from dynamic arguments for Hadamard products and linear relations. Wang et al. handle the latter in the particular case of a permutation matrix, via a sparse argument---a protocol whose prover runs in time proportional to the Hamming weight of the witness. Nevertheless, their techniques do not directly extend to the arbitrary matrices arising in constraint systems such as R1CS or CCS. Furthermore, the standard approach for proving general linear relations is unsuitable for the sparse setting because of a witness-independent step: the prover commits to an auxiliary polynomial determined by the matrices alone, and is hence dense regardless of how sparse the witness might be.

Our first contribution is a sparse zkSNARK for linear relations, which we build from a fully witness-dependent argument together with what we call a rational encoding of the matrices. As our second contribution, we develop a compiler that turns any sparse argument for a linear relation into a dynamic one, while preserving the zero-knowledge property of the underlying scheme.

Instantiated for Plonk and R1CS-lite, our techniques yield universal dynamic zkSNARKs with at most $20$ group elements per proof and $23$ verifier pairings---over $6.5\times$ and $7.8\times$ fewer than the state of the art---as well as asymptotically faster updates. We also show how both of our constructions can be de-amortized.

1    Introduction
Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs) are central to modern cryp-
tography, enabling scalable blockchain architectures and privacy-preserving protocols. Despite a rich variety
of constructions [Gro16,GWC19,CHM+ 20,Set20,GLS+ 23,NS24,ACFY25] built from different techniques and
assumptions, nearly all zkSNARKs are strictly static: updating a proof π for an instance-witness pair (x, w) to
a proof π ′ for a slightly modified pair (x′ , w′ ) requires re-executing the full proving algorithm from scratch—
even if (x, w) and (x′ , w′ ) differ by just one bit.
    Dynamic zkSNARKs, introduced by Wang, Papamanthou, Srinivasan and Papadopoulos [WPSP26b],
address this inefficiency. They extend standard zkSNARKs with an Update algorithm that produces an
updated proof π ′ in time sublinear in the statement size, provided the Hamming distance between (x, w)
and (x′ , w′ ) is small. The primitive is useful whenever the same statement is proved repeatedly while its
witness changes only locally, as when a large data set is certified to satisfy some property and a few of
its records are subsequently edited. Dynamic zkSNARKs also imply other cryptographic primitives, such
as sparse zkSNARKs—where proving time scales with the Hamming weight of the witness—and bounded
incremental verifiable computation without recursion [WPSP26b].

Limitations of Existing Constructions. Existing dynamic zkSNARKs fall into two categories, and suffer
from a sharp trade-off between universality and concrete efficiency.
 1. Circuit-specific constructions. Dynark [ZOZ26] and Delphus [WPSP26a] build on top of
    Groth16 [Gro16]. While concretely efficient, they inherit Groth16’s main drawback: reliance on a
    non-universal, circuit-specific trusted setup. Delphus is moreover restricted to the designated-verifier
    setting.
 2. Universal constructions. The protocols of [WPSP26b] support universal setups, but at a severe cost:
    in the most efficient variant the verifier requires over 180 pairings and the prover commits to more than
    130 polynomials, despite achieving asymptotically constant proof size and verification time. Furthermore,
    these numbers are lower bounds: [WPSP26b] focus on the non-zero-knowledge, non-universal variants of
    their protocols, only sketching universality and zero-knowledge. Moreover, they present their construction
    using symmetric pairings, for which no efficient instantiation is known at standard security levels. Finally,
    their constructions are tied to a restricted variant of the Plonk constraint system that lacks support for
    basic operations such as multiplication by public constants.

This leads to our first research question.

       Can we construct universal dynamic zkSNARKs that are concretely efficient and support standard
                                            constraint systems?

The core building block of [WPSP26b] is a sparse permutation argument: given a permutation σ, it proves
that aℓ = aσ(ℓ) for all ℓ in time proportional to the Hamming weight of a. Permutation arguments are
what Plonk-style systems need, which is why the constructions of [WPSP26b] are confined to that family.
The other widely used constraint systems, such as R1CS-lite [CFF+ 21], instead rely on a lincheck protocol
proving a matrix-vector relation M a = b. Supporting them would therefore require a sparse lincheck, but
the techniques of [WPSP26b] are specific to permutations. This motivates our second research question.

                            Can we construct sparse zkSNARKs for linear relations?


1.1     Our Contributions

Our answer to the second question is affirmative for a class of matrices that we argue is essentially the largest
possible, and it yields an affirmative answer to the first as well. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

    • Sparse zkSNARKs for linear relations. Our central contribution is a sparse zkSNARK for relations
      M (j) a = b(j) , j ∈ [l], where each matrix has at most V (j) non-zero entries per column. This restriction
      on the matrix structure is natural, and a similar assumption was made in [ZOZ26]: if a column of M (j)
      is dense, b(j) can easily result in a dense vector even when a is highly sparse. We build this protocol
      by replacing standard matrix-dependent dense lincheck polynomials with witness-dependent auxiliary
      polynomials that preserve the sparsity.
    • A compiler from sparse to dynamic, with zero-knowledge. We give a compiler turning any sparse
      zkSNARK for a linear relation into a dynamic one. The natural way of updating a proof exploits linearity:
      the difference of the original and the updated statement is again a valid statement of the relation, which
      can be proven with the sparse zkSNARK. However, a naive application does not result in zero-knowledge:
      it is possible to distinguish between fresh and updated proofs. Our solution again exploits linearity and
      consists of making the prover interpret its statement as an update to itself. This way, the distribution of
      fresh and updated proofs will be the same by construction.
    • Concretely efficient universal dynamic zkSNARKs. Combining the above with the dynamic ar-
      gument for Hadamard products of [ZOZ26], we obtain universal dynamic zkSNARKs for the standard
      Plonk constraint system [GWC19] and for a variant of R1CS-lite for circuits of bounded fan-out3 [RZ21].
      Compared to [WPSP26b] (see Table 1), the prover sends 20 commitments instead of more than 130 and
      the verifier performs 23 pairings instead of more than 180, improvements of 6.5× and 7.8×; we also
      improve the update complexity asymptotically in both the semi-dynamic and the fully-dynamic settings,
      and achieve the latter in the de-amortized setting.

1.2     Related Work
To the best of our knowledge, the only works on general purpose dynamic zkSNARKs are [WPSP26b], [ZOZ26]
and [WPSP26a], listed in Table 3 with their complexities. The dynamic zkSNARK of [ZOZ26] is fully
compatible with Groth16: it shares the same trusted setup, prover and verifier. The one of [WPSP26a]
diverges from Groth16 and requires a designated verifier.
    Wang et al. [WPSP26b] present two4 universal dynamic zkSNARKs: Dynalog and Dynaverse. Dynalog
relies on a hierarchical data structure to achieve polylogarithmic update times, but its proof size and verifier
time are polylogarithmic as well. Next we compare in detail with Dynaverse, which remains the most directly
comparable universal dynamic zkSNARK to our work.

Comparison with Dynaverse [WPSP26b]. Dynaverse uses a variant of the Plonk constraint system.
It encodes an arithmetic circuit with n addition and n multiplication gates using a redundant trace z =
(s1 , . . . , s6 ) ∈ F6n , and circuit satisfiability requires four checks: (i) correct wiring via a permutation σ, so
that zi = zσ(i) ; (ii) addition gate validity s1,i + s2,i = s3,i ; (iii) multiplication gate validity s4,i s5,i = s6,i ;
and (iv) consistency checks ensuring that each st is the correct subvector of z. We highlight the differences
with our constructions and give the full comparison of our schemes against it in Table 1.
    • Constraint system flexibility. The constraint system used by Dynaverse lacks support for basic
      operations such as addition or multiplication by public constants, so these must be encoded explicitly as
      part of the instance. This inflates the witness length and degrades efficiency. Using the standard Plonk
      and R1CS-lite constraint systems, we avoid this overhead entirely.
    • Linear constraints. To prove (i), Dynaverse relies on Dynamo, a sparse permutation argument. We
      extend its underlying idea to a much broader class of linear relations, and in doing so also handle several
      matrices at once.
    • Non-linear constraints. For (iii), Dynaverse uses an “anchor” technique: the updater shows that the
      multiplication gates hold in the updated coordinates only, and pairs this with a static anchor proof. We
      instead adapt the protocol of [ZOZ26], which is simpler, achieves an optimal proof size of a single group
      element, and improves the asymptotics of updates in the fully-dynamic setting.
    • Expensive consistency checks. In Dynaverse the consistency checks (iv) account for roughly two
      thirds of both the proof size and the verifier’s pairings. They appear inherent to Plonk-style systems:
      the sparse permutation argument operates on the full extended witness,5 whereas the gate constraints
      apply locally to the individual wire vectors. Our Plonk construction faces the same structural problem
      but resolves it differently: instead of enforcing subvector correctness with a dedicated and expensive
      protocol, we express the relation between the extended witness and the wire vectors as cyclic shifts—
      which are particularly structured linear maps—and our linear argument batches them together with
      the permutation into a single check. The consistency checks thus cost nothing in proof size or verifier
      pairings. Our R1CS-lite construction avoids them altogether, by the nature of the constraint system.
    • De-amortization. Because Dynaverse relies on the anchor technique, its update complexities hold only
      in an amortized sense: proofs can be updated efficiently as long as the new witness stays close to the
      anchor witness, and once that distance is exceeded it becomes cheaper to recompute the proof from
      scratch and amortize the cost over the previous updates. Our dynamic linear arguments use a similar
      anchor technique, but we de-amortize them following [ZOZ26].
Finally, a smaller proof does not in general mean a faster prover—multilinear zkSNARKs often outperform
univariate ones despite larger proofs. In this setting, however, the two go together: updating a proof re-
duces essentially to computing and sending KZG commitments [KZG10] to sparse polynomials, so fewer
commitments directly means faster updates.

From sparse lincheck to dynamic lincheck. Given a sparse lincheck, we build a dynamic one as follows.
Suppose the prover holds a valid proof π for M a = b and wants a proof for M a′ = b′ . The updater forms the
difference vectors a∗ = a′ − a and b∗ = b′ − b and produces a proof π ∗ for M a∗ = b∗ . The cost of π ∗ scales
with the sparsity of a∗ , which is exactly the Hamming distance between a and a′ . The updated proof consists
of the commitments to a∗ and b∗ , the difference proof π ∗ , and the original proof π; by linearity, a verifier
accepting both π and π ∗ is convinced that M a′ = b′ . In the language of [ZOZ26] this is a semi-dynamic
SNARK, one that can update proofs produced by Prove but not proofs produced by Update; a compiler
from [ZOZ26] turns it into a fully-dynamic SNARK, i.e., one that can update proofs regardless of how they
were generated.

The zero-knowledge problem, and how we solve it. The construction just described is not zero-knowledge, and
the reason is structural rather than a matter of blinding: a proof produced by Prove is a single sparse proof,
whereas a proof produced by Update additionally carries the difference commitments and a second sparse
proof. The two are distinguishable at a glance, however zero-knowledge the underlying sparse argument may
be.
    Our solution is that the prover should never prove the statement it is given, but a re-randomisation of
it. Concretely, Prove samples a random opening of the zero vector, subtracts it from the statement, and
proves the resulting re-randomised statement; the difference between the two is then a commitment to the
zero vector with uniformly random opening, which is distributed exactly like the difference commitments of
a genuine update. Since a fresh proof is now the update of a statement to itself, fresh and updated proofs
are produced by the same algorithm and are identical in shape by construction, and zero-knowledge of the
compiled scheme follows from that of the sparse argument alone.

2.1     Semi-dynamic zkSNARKs
Next, we introduce the notion of universal semi-dynamic zkSNARK [ZOZ26]. Intuitively, a zkSNARK is semi-
dynamic if it is possible to update proofs output by Prove, but not necessarily those output by Update. In
contrast, a fully-dynamic zkSNARK (or simply, a dynamic zkSNARK) ensures that proofs can be updated,
independently of how they were generated. The formal definition of fully-dynamic zkSNARK is given in
Section A. We also remark that there is one main difference between the zero-knowledge notion of [ZOZ26]
and the one from [WPSP26b]. For [WPSP26b], zero-knowledge means that a proof reveals no information
about the witness; for [ZOZ26], it is additionally required that proofs generated by the Prove algorithm are
indistinguishable from those generated by Update. We will focus on the stronger definition of [ZOZ26].

The standard definition of zkSNARK can be easily recovered from the definition of semi-dynamic zkSNARK
and is therefore omitted. Next, we give the formal definition of sparse zkSNARK as given in [WPSP26b],
which are zkSNARKs where the prover complexity scales with the Hamming weight of the witness.
Definition 4 (Sparse zkSNARK). A zkSNARK is sparse if there exists a function f (|x|+|w|) = o(|x|+|w|)
such that for all 0 ≤ k ≤ |x| + |w|, the running time of Prove(pki , x, w) is O(kf (|x| + |w|)), where k is the
Hamming weight of (x, w).

From semi-dynamic to fully-dynamic. The work of [ZOZ26] gives a compiler that turns semi-dynamic
zkSNARKs into fully-dynamic ones in the de-amortized setting. Intuitively, the updater needs to compute
the new proof and part of the new data during each proof update. For this to work, we need to assume that
the BuildData algorithm can be computed stepwise, across a fixed number of b steps. Let us explain in more
detail.
    Assume that the prover holds a sequence of instance-witness pairs ((x0 , w0 ), (x1 , w1 ), ...) for which it wants
to generate proofs. We will further assume that the Hamming distance between (xj , wj ) and (xj+1 , wj+1 ) is
at most k, for some small value k 7 . Throughout, k always denotes this distance; when we need to refer to the
sparsity of the base witness on which BuildData is run we write k0 instead. This way, the prover can generate a
base proof for (x0 , w0 ) by running π0 ← Prove(pki , x0 , w0 ), and compute data ← BuildData(pki , x0 , w0 , rand) in
order to be able to use (x0 , w0 ) as a base instance-witness pair for further updates. Specifically, an updater can
then run Update(pki , x0 , w0 , xj , wj , π0 , data) to obtain subsequent proofs. Observe that the further the updated

A     Definition of Universal Fully Dynamic zkSNARKs

In this section we provide the definition of universal fully-dynamic zkSNARKs. The fundamental difference
with respect to the semi-dynamic definition is that now, the proofs output by the Update algorithm can be
updated too, and not just the ones given by Prove.

Definition 14. A universal fully-dynamic zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge
(universal fully-dynamic zk-SNARK) for an indexed relation R consists of the following PPT algorithms
Π = (KeyGen, Derive, BuildData, Prove, Update, Verify):

 – KeyGen(1λ ) → (srs = (pk, vk), trap): On input the security parameter 1λ , outputs the universal structured
   reference string srs containing the universal prover key pk, a verifier key vk and a trapdoor trap needed
   for simulation.
 – Derive(i, srs) → srsi = (pki , vki ): On input an index i and the universal structured reference string srs,
   outputs specialized structured reference string srsi containing the specialized prover key pki and verifier
   key vki .
 – Prove(pki , x, w) → (π, rand): On input the specialized prover key pki , valid extended witness (i, x, w) ∈ R,
   outputs the proof π and randomness rand.
 – BuildData(pki , x, w, rand) → data: On input specialized prover key pki , instance x, witness w and random-
   ness rand, outputs a data structure data used for updates.
 – Update(pki , x, w, x′ , w′ , π, data, rand) → (π ′ , data′ , rand′ ): On input the specialized prover key pki , valid
   extended witnesses (i, x, w), (i, x′ , w′ ) ∈ R, proof π, preprocessed data data, and randomness rand, outputs
   an updated proof π ′ , updated preprocessed data data′ and updated randomness rand′ .
 – Verify(vki , x,π) → 0/1: On input the specialized verifier key vki , instance x and proof π output by Prove
   or Update, outputs accept or reject.
